narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 55.9% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. The strongest influence was your plan to attend law school part-time. Most students who are accepted (nearly 93%) plan to study full-time. Your part-time status pushed the prediction noticeably toward failure, as the model has learned that balancing work and intensive bar preparation is often more challenging.

Next in importance were your LSAT score of 33.5 and your undergraduate GPA of 3.3. Both of these actually worked in your favor. Your GPA is slightly above the average of accepted students, and your LSAT, while below the accepted average of 37.2, still pulled the prediction toward passing. However, these positive effects were not strong enough to overcome the impact of part-time enrollment.

Your first- and third-year college performance also sat below the averages of accepted students, adding some additional concern, but they were not among the top drivers.

You should consider reapplying with a plan to attend full-time. Strengthening your LSAT score would further improve your chances. Many students in similar situations have successfully gained admission and passed the bar after making these adjustments.
